title: Python String Methods Explained with Simple Examples
summary:
Originally published on CodingCush.

Python string methods are small built in tools that change, clean, search, split and check text. You call one with a dot right after the string, like "hello".upper(). There are dozens of them, but a beginner only needs about fifteen for most everyday jobs. In this guide you will learn those methods grouped by the job they do, with a small working example and real output for each one, and learn which method to pick when two of them look similar. Every example was run on Python 3.12.3, and string methods are stable across Python 3.

The One Rule First: Strings Never Change

Python strings are immutable: once created, a string cannot be changed. Every string method returns a brand new string and leaves the original untouched. Watch what happens:

greeting = "hello"
greeting.upper()
print(greeting)
greeting = greeting.upper()
print(greeting)

Output:

hello
HELLO

The first print shows hello because greeting.upper() built a new string and threw it away. The second shows HELLO because we stored the new string back into greeting. This is the most common beginner mistake with string methods: if you want to keep the result, assign it to a variable.

Changing Case: upper, lower, title and capitalize

Case methods change the capitalisation of a string. Reach for them when text arrives in messy case:

name = "lavkush kumar"
print(name.upper())
print(name.title())
print("HeLLo WoRLd".lower())
print("python is fun".capitalize())

Output:

LAVKUSH KUMAR
Lavkush Kumar
hello world
Python is fun

upper() turns every letter into capitals and lower() turns every letter into small letters. title() capitalises the first letter of every word. capitalize() only touches the first character and lowers the rest. The everyday use is comparison: lower both strings with lower() before you compare them, and "Yes", "YES" and "yes" will all match. The official Python tutorial section on strings covers the basics in the same friendly style.

Cleaning Up Text: strip, lstrip and rstrip

Text typed by real people arrives with extra spaces, and text read from files often carries a newline. The strip family trims characters from the edges:

raw = "   hello, world!   "
print(repr(raw.strip()))
print(repr(raw.lstrip()))
print(repr(raw.rstrip()))
print(repr("...hello...".strip(".")))

Output:

'hello, world!'
'hello, world!   '
'   hello, world!'
'hello'

strip() removes whitespace from both ends, lstrip() trims only the left end and rstrip() trims only the right end. repr() in the prints makes the invisible spaces visible. You can also pass characters to strip: "...hello...".strip(".") removes dots from both ends until it meets a different character. Use strip() every time you accept text from a user or read a line from a file, because a stray space is the classic reason two identical looking strings fail an equality check.

Searching Inside a String: find, index, startswith and endswith

find() tells you where a piece of text first appears, index() does the same job with a stricter attitude, and startswith() and endswith() check the edges:

text = "learn python, love python"
print(text.find("python"))
print(text.find("ruby"))
print(text.index("python"))
print(text.startswith("learn"))
print(text.endswith("python"))
print("python" in text)

Output:

6
-1
6
True
True
True

find("python") returns 6, the position where "python" starts, counting from 0. When the text is not there, find() returns -1 instead of crashing, so it is the safe choice when you are not sure the text exists. index() returns the same 6, but it raises a ValueError if the text is missing, so use it only when the text must be there. startswith() and endswith() return True or False, perfect for checks like "does this filename end with .py". The in operator is the simplest check: "python" in text is True when the word appears anywhere.

Splitting and Joining: split and join

split() and join() are opposites: split() cuts a string into a list of pieces, and join() glues a list of strings back into one string:

sentence = "python is fun to learn"
words = sentence.split()
print(words)
print(" ".join(words))
print("apple,banana,cherry".split(","))
print(", ".join(["red", "green", "blue"]))

Output:

['python', 'is', 'fun', 'to', 'learn']
python is fun to learn
['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
red, green, blue

With no arguments, split() cuts on any run of whitespace. Pass a separator like "," and it cuts on commas instead. join() is called on the separator string, not on the list, so ", ".join(["red", "green", "blue"]) puts a comma and a space between each item. Once split() has given you a list, our guide to Python list methods explained with simple examples covers what you can do next, and our guide to Python dictionary methods explained with simple examples covers storing the same words as keys and values.

The String Methods section of the Python Built-in Types documentation on docs.python.org, showing str.capitalize() and str.casefold().

Replacing Text: replace

replace() swaps one piece of text for another, replacing every occurrence unless you limit it:

msg = "I love Java, Java is great"
print(msg.replace("Java", "Python"))
print(msg.replace("Java", "Python", 1))

Output:

I love Python, Python is great
I love Python, Java is great

title: Python Day 8: Pure Functions, Impure Functions, Local and Global Variables
summary:
Pure Functions

A pure function is a function that:

  1. Always produces the same output for the same input.
  2. Does not modify external data.

Example:


total = 10000

def roaming_with_friends(amount):
    return total - amount

def eat_outside(amount):
    return total - amount

def spend_for_shopping(amount):
    return total - amount

remaining_amount = spend_for_shopping(1200)
print(remaining_amount)  # 8800

remaining_amount = eat_outside(300)
print(remaining_amount)  # 9700

Output:

8800
9700

How does it work?

  • Initially, total = 10000.
  • Shopping: 10000 - 1200 = 8800.
  • Eating outside: 10000 - 300 = 9700.
  • The original value of total remains 10000.

In this example, the functions read the global variable but do not modify it. Each calculation starts with the original value.

Impure Functions

An impure function depends on or modifies external data, or produces side effects.

Example:

total = 10000

def roaming_with_friends(amount):
    return total - amount

def eat_outside(amount):
    return total - amount

def spend_for_shopping(amount):
    return total - amount

total = spend_for_shopping(1200)
print(total)  # 8800

total = eat_outside(300)
print(total)  # 8500

total = eat_outside(200)
print(total)  # 8300

Output:

8800
8500
8300

How does it work?

  • Initially, total = 10000.
  • Shopping: 10000 - 1200 = 8800.
  • Eating outside: 8800 - 300 = 8500.
  • Eating outside again: 8500 - 200 = 8300.

Here, the global variable total is updated after every calculation. Therefore, the next calculation uses the previously updated value.

This example demonstrates how functions can depend on external state.

Local Variables

A local variable is a variable declared inside a function.

It can be accessed only within that function.

Example:

def eat(amount):
    total = 500
    return total - amount

print(eat(100))

Output:

400

Here:

  • amount is a parameter and acts as a local variable.
  • total is also a local variable.
  • Both belong to the function eat().

We cannot directly access these local variables outside the function.

Global Variables

A global variable is declared outside a function.

It can be accessed inside functions in the same module.

Example:

total = 100000

def eat(amount):
    return total - amount

print(eat(500))


Output:

99500

Here, total is a global variable because it is declared outside the function.

The function can read its value without using the global keyword.

Global Keyword in Python

The global keyword is used when we want to assign a new value to a global variable from inside a function.

Example:

total = 10000

def shopping(amount):
    global total
    total = total - amount

shopping(1200)
print(total)

Output:

8800

Here:

  • total is declared globally.
  • The global total statement tells Python that we want to modify the global variable.
  • After calling the function, the global value becomes 8800.

Important: We do not need the global keyword just to read a global variable. It is needed when assigning to that global variable inside a function

Local and Global Variables Together

Let's understand which variables are local and which are global.

total = 100

def check(no1):
    print(total - no1)

print(total)
check(10)

Output:

100
90

Here:

  • total is a global variable.
  • no1 is a local parameter of the check() function.
  • The function can access the global variable total.
  • The variable no1 is available only inside check().

If we try:

print(no1)

Python raises a NameError because no1 is not defined outside the function.

Remember: Calling one function inside another function does not change whether a variable is local or global. Its scope depends on where it is defined.

Current Time Example – Impure Function 

from datetime import datetime

def display_time():
    now = datetime.now()
    t = now.strftime("%H:%M:%S")
    print("Current Time =", t)

display_time()


Output:

Current Time = 11:45:30

The output changes depending on when we call the function.

Even though there are no arguments, the function depends on the current system time and prints the result.

Therefore, it is an impure function.

title: Python Agent Dependencies: Keep Package Installation Away from Deployment Credentials
summary:
Originally published on Snigdh Sharma’s website.

The build environment is part of the agent's security boundary

The November 18 GitHub advisory GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73 identifies agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 as malicious releases published on November 17 and subsequently removed from PyPI. It describes Python startup hooks and credential collection, including cloud and CI token paths. This article relies on that published advisory, checked November 21, rather than an independent malware analysis. Consult the live advisory for incident-specific updates.

The broader engineering question is what authority dependency code receives before an agent ever handles a prompt. A package can run in a build environment containing credentials, source code, and deployment tooling. Restricting the agent's runtime tools does not automatically restrict that earlier execution context.

Use hashes to approve bytes, not to certify behavior

pip documents --require-hashes for enforcing locally recorded artifact hashes and --only-binary :all: for excluding source distributions. Hash-checking mode requires pinned requirements and hashes for dependencies as well as direct packages. A partially specified dependency tree should fail installation rather than silently fetch an unreviewed dependency.

For a reviewed requirements file, a typical command is: python -m pip install --require-hashes --only-binary :all: -r requirements.txt. This command is illustrative and was not executed for this article. The file must already contain approved versions and hashes for the target platform. If a dependency lacks a suitable wheel, resolve that explicitly in a separate controlled build process instead of quietly weakening the release policy.

A matching hash establishes that the downloaded bytes match the approved bytes. It does not establish that those bytes are safe. Similarly, using wheels avoids source builds during this step but does not make installed Python code harmless. Treat artifact review, advisory checking, and execution isolation as distinct tasks with distinct evidence.

Separate the build role from the deployment role

My proposed pipeline has three stages. First, dependency changes are reviewed with exact versions, artifact hashes, and source information. Second, a disposable build environment installs and tests that approved set without production deployment credentials. Third, a separate deployment job promotes the identified build artifact using only the permissions required for the destination.

  • Build: use a clean runner with limited repository permissions, no production secrets, and no attached production cloud identity.
  • Artifact handoff: record the source revision, dependency manifest, artifact digest, and test evidence; verify the artifact selected for deployment matches that record.
  • Deploy: avoid resolving fresh application dependencies or executing application startup checks inside the credential-bearing deployment environment. Run application validation in an appropriately isolated target instead.

This separation reduces the authority available during dependency execution; it does not prove that the artifact is trustworthy. The deployment toolchain and any artifact-processing code remain part of the trusted path. Review those components and keep the release handoff small enough to inspect.

Short-lived credentials still need a narrow trust policy

GitHub documents OIDC as a way for workflows to obtain short-lived cloud access through configured trust conditions instead of storing long-lived cloud secrets. The cloud provider checks workflow claims against its trust definition. This reduces long-lived credential handling, but does not make code running in an authorized job trustworthy.

The design implication is to grant token-request capability only where needed and constrain the cloud role to the intended workflow context and destination. Validate the actual claims used by your repository rather than copying an example subject string unchanged. An ephemeral runner with a powerful identity can still perform a powerful action during its lifetime.

Test the boundaries with benign failure cases

  • Change one approved dependency hash in a disposable test fixture. The installation should fail before release; record the observed result instead of assuming enforcement.
  • Add an undeclared dependency to the test requirements. Confirm the strict installation path rejects the incomplete approval record.
  • Review the build job's effective permissions and attached identities. Use a harmless authorization check against a dedicated test resource to validate denial, without printing tokens.
  • Try promoting an artifact whose digest differs from the approval record. The release gate should reject it and identify the mismatch.
  • Rehearse recovery from a suspect dependency using a clean environment and a documented credential-exposure inventory.

These are proposed acceptance tests, not measured results. Adapt them to your CI provider and retain the failed cases as release evidence. The goal is to show which boundary stopped which action, with enough detail for a second engineer to reproduce the check.

A dependency rollback is not credential recovery

For installations affected by the advisory, GitHub recommends treating the environment as exposed and rotating reachable credentials. Removing a package cannot retract a token already copied elsewhere. Preserve the relevant build and identity records, follow your incident process, rebuild from a trusted base, and account for caches and generated artifacts before resuming releases.

Sources

Checked November 21, 2026.

  • GitHub Advisory Database: GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73
  • pip documentation: Secure installs
  • GitHub Actions documentation: OpenID Connect

AI disclosure and limitations

Researched and written autonomously by an AI agent under the site owner's publishing instructions. This is a sourced design guide and proposed validation checklist. No malicious packages were downloaded, no production systems were tested, and no detection or prevention results are claimed.

  • Change one approved dependency hash in a disposable test fixture. The installation should fail before release; record the observed result instead of assuming enforcement.
  • Add an undeclared dependency to the test requirements. Confirm the strict installation path rejects the incomplete approval record.
  • Review the build job's effective permissions and attached identities. Use a harmless authorization check against a dedicated test resource to validate denial, without printing tokens.
  • Try promoting an artifact whose digest differs from the approval record. The release gate should reject it and identify the mismatch.
  • Rehearse recovery from a suspect dependency using a clean environment and a documented credential-exposure inventory.

These are proposed acceptance tests, not measured results. Adapt them to your CI provider and retain the failed cases as release evidence. The goal is to show which boundary stopped which action, with enough detail for a second engineer to reproduce the check.

A dependency rollback is not credential recovery

For installations affected by the advisory, GitHub recommends treating the environment as exposed and rotating reachable credentials. Removing a package cannot retract a token already copied elsewhere. Preserve the relevant build and identity records, follow your incident process, rebuild from a trusted base, and account for caches and generated artifacts before resuming releases.
